- **WATER RUDDER, RETRACTED AND DEPLOYED, IN THE FLOAT'S WAKE AND IN A CURRENT (Claude, 2026-11-05 03:50; Ty 2026-11-04
  20:28, merge pre-approved). lane/claude-wheel-hydroplane 53935b58 → island-nav 6124b5a3 → Quest 17126885. iOS
  2026.1105.0335 ** BUILD SUCCEEDED **, 0 error CS, installed on the EFB iPad and the iPad mini (the iPhone was not
  attached; one launch refused because the iPad was locked). Quest 2026.1105.0343, 0 error CS, installed and launched on
  the Quest 3S. check-parity: PARITY OK. Nothing approved by me.**
  - **What changed (FloatHydro.DrawnWaterRudder, HeelWake).** The blade is still the drawn elliptic plate cut into cells
    against the water. Each wet cell now takes ITS OWN flow: V + ω×r at the cell, through the water, minus what the
    float's turbulent boundary layer, shed off the heel, carries along there. δ = 0.37·L·Re^−0.2 and u/U = (d/δ)^(1/7)
    (Schlichting), where d is the distance to the heel's WETTED outline, traced back along the stream. Lift per cell
    uses that cell's angle and ½ρw²; induced drag is taken on the whole blade. The lever position (0.8 s slew, or a VR
    hand) is the same geometry at another angle, not a blend: half-up gives 681 N·m against 854 down and 71 up. The
    PA-18/Beaver lumped blade takes the same wake at its centre.
  - **Numbers, J-3 at rest attitude, 3 m/s, full pedal swing:** lowered 854 N·m (u/U 0.999, 168.5 N lift vs 168.9 in
    open water). Hooked 71 N·m, 8 % of lowered: only 0.0114 m² stays wet and it sits in the heel's wake at u/U 0.88.
    That was 89 N·m without the wake. Idle full-pedal turn unchanged: 254° up, 259° down in 20 s.
  - **Current:** from lane/claude-river-current (merged earlier, bae2eeae). Moored in a 3 m/s current, the blade gives
    exactly what it gives taxiing at 3 m/s in still water, lowered and hooked; drifting with the current it gives zero.
    The blade uses the float's current at the step, not its own depth.
  - **Decision (Q056):** the model's float ends in a flat 27 × 21 cm heel. I did NOT model a dead-water core behind it.
    That core would leave the hooked blade with ~0 authority straight ahead (it would steer only in a swing). Keep it as
    now, or add the core? Please fly the J-3 on floats with the rudder hooked and lowered.
  - Tests: J3WaterRudderWakeTests (new, 5: formula literals worked by hand, hooked-in-wake, between the stops, wake lies
    downstream, current). Two J3WaterRudderTests literals now use the cells' q̄. 30/30 for J3WaterRudder* +
    WaterCurrentTests. The Float/Hydro/Water subset shows 17 failures on the branch AND the same 17 on the branch point
    3181743c (world-water tests: waterfalls, lakes, glaciers); nothing new.

- **1 Crash reset.** Cause: the sim was always fresh. The wreck lived on in the DRAWN model: AirframeVisual only rebuilt a
  damaged model when the new aeroplane had lost nothing a frame later, and a bent wing panel set no flag (old
  AirframeVisual.cs ~60 / ~80-85), so a same-type Restart kept the wreck drawn. Fix: FlightSimDriver.AirframeReplaced
  (raised from the Sim setter on every spawn path + AdoptSim) = the one reset; AirframeVisual.ShowsDamage rebuilds on it;
  StructuralDamage, FlightAudio, CrashWaterVisuals clear on it. **Persisted? No: force-quit + relaunch clears it**
  (Ty's iPhone prefs hold only set.* and support.lastCrash; NoCrashStateIsPersisted holds runtime code to that).
- **2 Snow dust.** Cause: ContactEffects' dust material (FlyingGame/UnlitTransparent) ignores the particle colour, so every
  puff was brown. Fix: FlyingGame/Spray (mist) + Core CrashDust.For(ContactPoint.SurfaceCode) (WorldTerrain.SurfaceAt at the
  contact): snow white, ice light grey chips, water blue-white spray, paved grey, gravel/dirt/sand brown, grass/pasture
  green-brown, unknown old brown.
- **3 C172 transparent cockpit.** Cause: not the yoke merges. AirframeModels.PickOwn drew our 172 only with "own models" on
  (off by default, off on Ty's phone), so he got the downloaded shell with no cabin. Fix: c172 in LiveryChoice.OwnModelAlways;
  nose first (Spec left), Spec.AtDatum, glass material (JSON-only GLB patch, geometry unchanged). The 6:49 PM render on
  0bb87c67 showed no cabin because that commit predates the C172 merge (879e0cd4). **Proof on head dd6b3229

- **4 Wreck slides too far.** Cause: AirframeContact.SlidingMu (every structure hard point and every WreckSim piece) was the
  FLOAT-KEEL table (grass 0.35, snow 0.10, ice 0.03): a 30 m/s wreck went 131 m on grass, 459 m on snow, 1.5 km on ice.
  Fix: a wreck table (a crumpled airframe gouges and ploughs): paved 0.60, gravel 0.75, dirt/sand 0.80, grass 0.65,
  pasture 0.75, snow 0.40, packed snow 0.30, ice 0.20. These are the upper half of accident-reconstruction drag-factor bands
  for a body sliding on its side or roof (asphalt 0.3-0.5, grass/dirt 0.5-0.8, packed snow 0.2-0.3, ice 0.1-0.2). A gear-up

## NEEDS YOU — CARDBOARD VR ON THE iPHONE 17 PRO (Claude, 2026-11-04 ~20:00 PST, lane/claude-vr-stereo-merge)
Ty 19:39: "I have the cardboard vr headsets for the iphone now". lane/codex-vr-stereo (lens-distortion compositor,
in-world HUD, frustum fix) is merged with lane/claude-vr-stereo; both lanes carry it. How to use it:
- **Turn it on (phone OUT of the viewer):** OPTIONS (top right) → **Controls** tab → tick **"VR (Cardboard headset):
  split screen, full head tracking"**. Only shown on a device with a gyro. The screen locks landscape-left (charge port
  to your RIGHT) and stops sleeping. Under the tick: **"Eye spacing (IPD)"** slider 55–75 mm (63 default) and a
  **"Recentre the view"** button. Close OPTIONS, then put the phone in the viewer.
- **It stays on across relaunch** (PlayerPrefs `vr.on`): the app reopens split-screen. Menus (landing page, OPTIONS)
  still draw FLAT across both halves on purpose so you can always turn VR off — but you must take the phone out to read
  or tap them. There is no in-headset menu on the phone (the Quest has one; Cardboard does not).
- **Flying in the headset needs a gamepad** (8BitDo/MFi/Xbox/PS via the Input System, `GamepadInput`; no profile
  needed) or a calibrated joystick. The touch controls are hidden, and as of this merge also INERT in VR, so a
  trigger press cannot hit an invisible RESET or BAIL. Gamepad Menu (Start) still opens OPTIONS (flat).
- **Recentre:** hold the screen / Cardboard trigger **0.6 s**, or click the gamepad's **right stick (R3)** (added in
  this merge; before, R3 only recentred the mono look), or the Options button.
- **No QR / viewer-profile scan.** The lens is fixed: generic Google Cardboard v2 (k1 0.336, k2 0.553, 63.9 mm lenses,
  39.3 mm screen-to-lens, 60° each way) from configs/vr-cardboard.json, copied to StreamingAssets at build. A viewer
  that is not a v2 needs its own numbers in that file. Screen size comes from Screen.dpi (326 dpi fallback).
- **Check on the headset:** image upright and fused; straight lines straight at the edges (distortion strength);
  red/blue fringe at the edges; HUD (IAS kt / ft MSL / heading, 1.5 m ahead, low) legible and comfortable; frame rate;
  where the trigger actually lands (it must not open OPTIONS, top right). Nothing here is approved.
- Validation: VrStereo+VrDistortion 52/52. Full suite 2487 passed / 216 failed (2709, 1 h 53 m, machine loaded); the 141
  failing methods re-run alone on the merge AND on base 0bb87c67 fail the identical 124 cases — nothing new. iOS export
  0 `error CS`, xcodebuild Release generic iOS `** BUILD SUCCEEDED **` (own output dirs, not installed). Quest: Cardboard
  cannot start there (`VrMode.Available` is false while `XrHeadset.Active`, the toggle is OnGUI-only and QuestMenu has no
  VR switch, so `vr.on` is never set); its shaders are plain CG in Resources. No Quest build was run for this merge.

- **Q026 ITEM 3: P-51 ROLLOUT PROP STRIKE AND SWIFT WATER SKIM, INVESTIGATED (Claude, 2026-11-04, lane/claude-tire-spinup).
  Nothing in the physics or configs was changed. You asked for findings first.**
  1. **The P-51's wheel mass is about right, and it is not the cause.**
     - Model: 30 kg rotating per main, r 0.343 m (a 27 in smooth contour), I = 0.65·m·r² = 2.29 kg·m².
     - Real: the tyre is 27 in on a **14 in rim** (DMI Aviation / Goodyear application chart). I found no published
       weight. My estimate is tyre 15–17 kg (a 26x10.5-6 6-ply is 10.4 kg; this one is bigger and 8–10 ply), plus
       tube, wheel and brake discs, about 28–31 kg. So **30 kg is plausible**.
     - **The inertia factor is probably ~25 % high for this wheel.** Much of the mass sits at the 14 in rim, not out
       at the tread: about 0.47 rather than the fleet's 0.65, so I ≈ 1.7 kg·m². That is an estimate, not a measurement.
     - **What actually happens:** the calm "three-point" landing touches down at 54 m/s, which is 1.13 × the model's
       Vso (the harness starts at 1.15 Vso, 5 ft) and **at 8° pitch against the 10.7° three-point attitude**. So it is a
       fast wheel landing. It rolls 3 s, the stick comes back above flying speed, and it balloons to 3.6 m. Two more
       bounces follow, and the third arrival is nose-low (−1.7°) and strikes. The prop clears by 1.24 m at rest and
       0.68 m level, so a strike needs a nose-down arrival, not just the spin-up kick.
     - **The branch point (b85ea02e, no spin-up) bounced too,** to 2.5 m and 1.1 m, and survived by luck.
     - **Sensitivity:** at 25 kg, or I 2.0, it passes. At 30 kg, or I 2.29, it strikes. That is the bounce sequence
       changing chaotically, not a margin that grows with the mass.
     - **My recommendation:** fix the arrival, not the wheel. Either the test pilot / landing law holds the P-51
       off to a real three-point (near Vso, ~11°), or I set `wheelInertiaKgM2` ≈ 1.7 on the P-51 mains from the
       rim-size estimate. Say which, or neither. `TaildraggerNoTipStrikeTests.NormalLanding…(p51d-like)` stays red.
  2. **The Swift water skim is emergent, and the test now says so.**
     - The real 300x100 monowheel (r 0.15 m) cannot plane at the 25 m/s touch. It ploughs at ~0.5 g for 1.5 s
       (dig-in 24.1 m/s at full weight), the nose dips in at ~17 m/s, and the nose joint breaks.
     - The break is from the water's load (`AirframeFlooding.CheckJoints`: 2.1 kN along the fuselage against
       9 g × the nose's own mass = 1.6 kN). It is not a water-touch trigger.
     - `WheelWaterTests.ALightTouchAtSpeedSkims…(glider-swift-s1-like)` now asserts your 20:24 rule instead of
       "breaks nothing": every lost part has a logged water load over its ultimate, and the wings hold. It is green.
     - **Open question:** the Swift's nose joint counts only the nose's own ~18 kg, not the pilot whose feet are in it.
       Is 1.6 kN too weak a glider nose? That is crash-water's joint rule (decision 1), so I did not touch it.
  3. **Water-touch crash triggers: owned by other lanes, so I did not duplicate them.**
     - SR22/Glasair: lane/claude-wheel-hydroplane 4bbfe5b5 makes the water prop strike emergent (blade drag on the
       rotor). Those two tests are still red here until it merges; they were red at the branch point too.
     - The full audit (no `surface == Water` crash; damage only from loads) is crash-reset follow-up item 4, queued.
     - What I checked in this lane: `AirframeContact` already leaves water breaks to the load path for everything but
       the propeller, and `TyreWear` / `WheelSpin` have no water trigger.
     - **Still to audit:** `CrashRelay.OnHardImpact` raises a `CrashImpact` on water above `WaterSplashMinMs` of
       closing speed. Whether that counts as a "crash" is for crash-reset's audit.
- **TYRE WEAR, BURST AND FLAT TYRES: MERGED INTO BOTH LANES AND INSTALLED (Claude, 2026-11-04/05, lane/claude-tire-spinup).
  iOS 2026.1104.2251 on the iPhone + iPad mini; Quest 2026.1105.0007 on the Quest 3S (see the Log entry "merge and installs").
  Ty's Q026 answer (20:21): keep the 172's full-pedal lock-up; item 2, the 0.222 m radius, is confirmed. iOS build
  2026.1104.2140 `** BUILD SUCCEEDED **`, 0 `error CS`, PARITY OK, not installed. No new red tests (below). Please fly it:**
  1. **The burst, Core `TyreWear`, emergent.** The model:
     - Wear = γ(T) × the wheel's own slip work, laid on the strips of tread under the patch.
     - T is the Blok flash temperature of the slide.
     - A tyre bursts when a strip is worn through, and goes flat in 0.15 s.

     Measured on the C172, idle, full pedal held:

     | Case | Wear | Result |
     |---|---|---|
     | Locked from 60 kt (flapless) | through | **bursts after 65 m of skid** |
     | Locked from 25 kt | 2.9 mm | flat spot, no burst |
     | Locked on grass from 55 kt | 0.38 mm | no burst |
     | 60 % pedal, no lock | 0.0003 mm | — |
     | Normal spin-up | 0.06 mm over a quarter of the tread | about 450 landings of tread |

     **One fitted constant:** the hot abradability, 1.0e-9 m³/J, set so a locked 6.00-6 at 38 psi goes through in ~60 m.
     Is that the right severity, or should a flapless lock-up survive more often?
  2. **The flat, all geometry.** The wheel stands on its rim plus two flattened casings, so:
     - the 172 sits **2.3° down** on that side;
     - it adds **~0.07 g of rolling drag** (+0.16 μr on that wheel);
     - the load on that wheel swings 28 % once a revolution as the worn-through strip passes under the axle.

     Steering on a flat is unchanged (cornering stiffness not modelled), and the wheel visual does not show the flat.
  3. **Sound and smoke, untested by ear:**
     - The screech is the existing skid voice.
     - New: a pop on burst, a ~70 Hz thump from the axle's work on the lumps, and a casing slap once per wheel revolution.
     - New `TyreSmoke`: particles in proportion to the rubber torn off, so a puff at each spin-up and a trail when locked.
     - **Levels and the smoke density need your eyes and ears.**
  4. Tyres are new again at every spawn/reset.

       - The cause is the spin-up nose-down impulse: two ~30 kg main assemblies at ~50 m/s, ≈ 16 deg/s on its I_yy.

       - Either the P-51's rotating mass is high, or its touchdown needs stick held harder back.

       rule gave 0.31) is too small to plane at 25 m/s, digs in, and the nose breaks off. It passes with the auto radius.

     (a) **Sinking — fixed.** The sim's wreck pieces rest at 0.0 cm on the runway and beside it for 12 s
         (`DebrisGroundTests`). What sank was the Unity fallback for a piece with no sim piece: it DELETED the piece when its
         origin (the aeroplane's CG at the break, well above the piece's lowest point) got within 0.3 m of the ground — the
         mesh half under the grass as it vanished. It now lands, slides (μ 0.5) and rests, and is never removed for

- **NEEDS YOU: APPROVE THE DEBRIS RENDERS. CRASH DEBRIS NOW COMES FROM THE AEROPLANE ON SCREEN, IN ITS LIVERY (Claude,
  2026-11-03, lane/claude-pitts-debris `0a5a7e79` repro + `b1c00bca` fix):** the prebuilt debris pieces are the
  Codex lane's (lane/codex-pitts-debris); their renders are in `~/Developer/agent-lanes/xfer/debris-v1/<aircraft>/` and
  `~/Developer/agent-lanes/xfer/pitts-debris-v1/`. **Nothing is installed**: no `*-debris.glb` is in Resources, and
  `DebrisWiringTests.NoDebrisSetIsInstalledBeforeTheRendersAreApproved` fails if one appears. Once you approve, put each set beside
  its intact GLB as `<intact GLB name>-debris.glb` (e.g. `Resources/Models/pitts-s2b-like/pitts-s2b-like-own-n1191-debris.glb`) and the
  game picks it up. Until then the runtime split below makes the pieces, from the same model and the same paint.
  - **Root cause** (two faults, `AirframeVisual.cs` at `ce53d62e`):
    1. `TryPlaceModel` (`:2114-2126`) hides the procedural shell but leaves its parts in `_parts`/`_wingParts`. `DetachStatic`
       (`:337-414`) and `DetachWings` (`:525-558`) split those parts too and hand every piece to `AddPiece` (`:580-590`), which gives it a
       NEW, ENABLED `MeshRenderer`. **That is the "old Pitts render"**: the red procedural Pitts's wings, ailerons, stab, fin, rudder,
       cowl, prop and wheels fell out in `FlyingGame/Airframe` paint. For the stab and fin, `Matches()` (`:308-320`) only knew the
       procedural names (the model's meshes are `Model:Stab`...). So a stab or fin loss dropped only the hidden shell's part, and the
       model's own tail stayed on the aeroplane.
    2. `CloneMesh` (`:661-669`) copied positions and triangles into submesh 0 and nothing else: no UVs, colours or tangents, and
       recomputed normals. `AddPiece` took only `mr.sharedMaterial` (slot 0). Every piece lost its baked texture paint, and so did the part
       left on the aeroplane, because the kept half went through the same copy. `CutModelLeg` (`:1681-1738`) kept uv0 but merged the
       submeshes into slot 0.
  - **Reproduced** by the new editor check `DebrisPaintCheck` on `0a5a7e79`: the Pitts failed in all 4 liveries (60 failures,
    `/tmp/pitts-debris/repro-base.log`); the whole fleet failed with 666 failures (`/tmp/pitts-debris/fleet-base.log`).
  - **Fix** (`b1c00bca`):
    - New `DebrisMesh.Split` carries every vertex attribute (normals, tangents, colours, all 8 UV channels) and keeps each triangle in its own
      submesh. `ForPiece` drops empty submeshes together with their materials. Every cut goes through it.
    - `AirframeBuilder.IsDebrisSource`: anything hidden when the model took over is never debris. Its lost parts still leave the
      airframe, unseen. A prop strike no longer bends the hidden shell's blades into visible cubes.
    - The model's own named parts match their component (Stab/Elevator/Fin/Rudder/Aileron_UL...). A one-mesh downloaded model's tail is cut
      from the space of the hidden procedural stab/fin. The model's mesh objects are emptied, never destroyed, so the J-3's elevators
      under its Stab and the rig nodes survive.
    - A wing failure no longer takes the stabiliser tips and wheels with it.
    - A nose or tail break after a wing failure now still cuts the model; `TakeWingParts` used to drop the whole model from the part
      list.
    - Wing and fin lettering (`Decal:*`) leaves with the wing or fin it is painted on.
    - **Prebuilt hook**: `TakePrebuiltDebris` loads `AirframeModels.PlacedResourcePath(id) + "-debris"`, which is the very file
      `Place` loaded, so it can never be another livery's or another type's. It is placed at the intact model's pose and drops its
      `Debris.<AirframeComponent>.<label>` nodes. The runtime split still takes the part off the aeroplane but drops nothing of its
      own. There is no lookup for the procedural shell, or for a model repainted at run time (the Talk Flying 172, a recoloured 2-33).
      Rebuild/livery change resets the hook.
    - Wreck physics is unchanged.
    - TODO: runtime cuts are not capped; the prebuilt sets are.
  - **Tests**:
    - `DebrisPaintCheck` (`Unity -batchmode -nographics -projectPath unity -executeMethod FlyingGame.EditorTools.DebrisPaintCheck.Run`,
      `DEBRIS_TYPES=` to limit) breaks every type up through the game's own code, in every livery and with own-models off and on, plus
      the 2-33 and 172 override schemes: the wing failure plus stab, fin, nose and both mains, then aileron, elevator, rudder, a whole
      wing, an outer panel, tail boom, tailwheel, nose gear and nose. Every debris face must be a face that was drawn, at the same
      place, with the same Material object and the same UV. Kept parts must keep their UVs. The prebuilt hook is exercised on every
      Pitts livery with a stand-in set cut from the intact GLB.
      **PASS: 48 of 48 (type, livery, file) combinations, 0 failures** (`/tmp/pitts-debris/fleet3.log`); base: 666 failures.
    - New `tools/FlightTests/DebrisWiringTests` (3 tests): the debris-set names per Pitts livery as literals, no set installed, and the
      wiring.
    - The targeted suites (DebrisWiring, LiveryPicker, OwnPittsModel): 26/26 passed.

- **FLOATS NO LONGER BREAK UP ON LANDING; WHEELS SKIM WATER FOR REAL — FLY TO CHECK, AND TWO DECISIONS (Claude,
  2026-11-03, lane/claude-wheel-hydroplane; 325b367e is in lane/claude-crash-physics, the follow-up is not; NOT installed.
  Build-ready: iOS `2026.1103.2246` ** BUILD SUCCEEDED **, 0 `error CS` — deploy.sh not run, as instructed).**
  - **Why the J-3 floats broke up:** the floats' planing lift (Savitsky) took its trim angle from the straight keel
    line just ahead of the step and gave ZERO lift at trim ≤ 0.1°, however much of the swept-up bow was in the water.
    Touch down flat or a little nose-low at speed (measured: 32 m/s, 2 m/s sink, −2°) and the floats knifed under
    (step draft 0.61 m on a 0.50 m float), it pitched to −10°, the engine hit the water at 70 mph and the engine-mount
    rule correctly tore the nose off ("12.4 kN along the fuselage against 12.1"). Fixed: below zero trim (only there —
    every positive-trim state, including the validated low-trim porpoise, is untouched) the trim moves over the first
    degree to the wetted bottom's chord, from the step keel to where the keel meets the water. At 60 mph, 100–300 fpm, +5° every landing was
    already clean, which is why the old test never saw it. Also fixed: an aeroplane spawned afloat took a phantom
    "slam" on its first step (the floats' entrained water counted as newly hit: 420 kN on a Beaver).
  - **DECISION 1 — hard-landing threshold (new: floats can now be damaged).** A float's bottom splits (that compartment
    floods; nothing breaks off) above its 14 CFR 23.527 ultimate water load: n_w = 0.012·V_S0²/(tan^⅔β·W^⅓) with each
    twin float the hull of a half-weight seaplane, ×1.5. J-3 floats: n_w 4.12 → 17.9 kN per float. Measured at 60 mph,
    +5°: up to 3.0 m/s (590 fpm) no damage, 3.5 m/s (690 fpm) splits both; the 23.473 design sink for this wing
    loading is 2.2 m/s (433 fpm): it peaks at 8.5 kN there. The water load is averaged over 20 ms (an assumed response
    time of a float on its struts — a one-step spike of the slam is not a load the struts feel). Worst normal landing
    in the tests (100 fpm, then a skip, wings held level): 12.5 of 17.9 kN; a fast flat touchdown 15.8. Landing on ONE
    float (wing low) is much harder — if you feel it splitting floats on landings you would call fair, say so. OK?

    ~20 kt (dig-in, full weight on the wheels) a tyre cannot hold itself up at all. The bushwheel option (half psi,
    twice the tyre) planes much lower. Want an 8.50-6 tundra option on the J-3 as its own setting?

- **WINGTIPS NO LONGER GO THROUGH THE GROUND; WING PANELS BEND AND BREAK; SLAVE STRUTS; PROP STRIKES — PLEASE
  FEEL-TEST (Claude, 2026-11-03, lane/claude-contact-patches). Nothing approved, NOT merged, NOT on any device**
  (`deploy.sh 00000000-NOINSTALL`: `** BUILD SUCCEEDED **`, 0 `error CS`, build 2026.1103.1656, installed nowhere).
  1. **Why the Pitts's tip went in:** its lower wing's strip heights already contain the dihedral (z 0.528 at the root
     → 0.408 at the tip) and the tip hard point subtracted |y|·tanΓ again: it sat **0.15 m inside the wing**, at the
     quarter chord only. Only the own-model biplanes' lower wings (Pitts, Great Lakes) are built like that; every other
     config keeps its strips flat, so the code now tells the two apart per surface (`WingStructure.ChordZ`).
  2. **Contact patches, fleet-wide:** every wing tip is a five-point patch (LE, TE, the aileron's outer trailing corner,
     lower and upper skin at 30 % chord), with ONE ground sample and ONE contact stiffness; stab tips, fin top (LE+TE),
     rudder heel; the propeller is its whole disc (12 blade-tip stations at full radius). Friction per island surface
     (hard structure sliding: paved 0.55, gravel 0.50, grass 0.35, snow 0.10, packed glacier 0.04 — the float keel's
     published coefficients; buildings 0.7). A wingtip is a cantilever (k_w = 3EI/L³) in series with the contact: the
     give is the wing flexing UP (drawn), not the ground coming through it.
  3. **Break stations** (the panel outboard bends/breaks): Pitts I-strut lower 2.18 / upper 2.28 m, Great Lakes N-strut
     2.875 m, J-3 lift-strut attach 3.40 m — all measured from our own model builders. **Not measured — the aileron's
     inboard end stands in:** Stearman, Jenny, C172, PA-18 ×3, Pawnee, Beaver ×2, AirCam ×2, 2-33 (marked
     `wingBracing: strut` where they are strut-braced, so their spar is still sized as a braced one). Cantilever types
     (Extra, P-51, jets …) use the aileron's inboard end by rule. **DONE 2026-11-03 (lane/claude-crash-physics, Ty
     decision 4: "decide it yourself"):** stations from cited references for every strut-braced type and both vintage
     biplanes, in the configs with `wingBreakStationSource`, pinned in `StrutStationTests` — table and sources in that
     lane's Log entry. Only the AirCam ×2 is still on the aileron-end rule (no published station found).
  4. **Strength from first principles, no fudge factors:** M1 = the Schrenk lift outboard of the station at 1 g less the
     panel's own weight (Raymer); a braced spar is one section from its root bay out, sized by that bay (q·L²/8). Limit =
     gMax × that (14 CFR 23.305: no permanent set below it); ultimate = limit × the game's ultimateFactor 2.0. Pitts
     lower panel: M1 72, bay 330, **limit 1,985, ultimate 3,971 N·m**. A strike moment between the two: **bent 5° tip-up,
     with the crunch** (raised through the crash-audio path); past ultimate: **off**, with its rows, its aileron, its mass
     and the CG shift. Measured, Pitts banked 35° at 20 m/s onto the lower tip: 0.8 m/s sink bends it, 3 m/s takes it.
  5. **Bent panel in flight (your rule):** 5° at 1 g, +10° per g, ratcheting (once at 10° it stays at 10°), snaps past 15°
     = 2 g. Test: held to 1.993 g, snapped at 2.014 g. **Against a real spar:** an intact Pitts lower panel turns ~0.06°
     per g at its station (a spar sized to its ultimate, σ/E ≈ 7·10⁻³ for spruce and 2024-T3 alike); the bent one turns
     10° per g — **~170× softer** — and it goes at 2·M1 = 143 N·m against the intact 3,971: **3.6 % of its strength
     left**. That is a spar that has broken through and is held by fabric, ribs and wires, not a "bent" one: a real spar
     that yields at limit and survives keeps most of its stiffness. It is your number, and it makes a bent panel very
     fragile on the ground too (item 10a).
  6. **Slave strut (Pitts):** a rigid link solved geometrically between horns on the lower (stick) and upper ailerons at
     the builder's stations, 10 in inboard of the I-struts. Never frozen: with both wings straight the uppers move
     exactly with the lowers (what the rig was solved with); a bent panel adds whatever the geometry changes. **The
     Pitts's struts pin INBOARD of the I-strut, so a lower-panel bend does not move them.** (A test with the pin moved
     outboard: a 5° bend drives the upper aileron ≈14° trailing-edge down and it still follows the stick.) **Geometry
     note:** the GLB's horns point opposite ways vertically; with the strut's 24° stagger lean that would move the uppers at
     only a fifth of the lowers. **DONE 2026-11-03 (lane/claude-crash-physics, Ty decision 5):** both horns now forward and
     20° below the chord (Pitts S-1-11 factory drawing, Detail A), parallel, in the sim (`SlaveLink.Build`, config
     `drivenHornDownDeg`/`slavedHornDownDeg`) and in `build_pitts_s2b.py` v13: uppers follow 1:1 within 0.11° over ±25°.
     The committed GLBs are NOT yet rebuilt (see that lane's NEEDS YOU).
  7. **Lower panel gone:** its aileron goes too (its hinge crossed the station), the strut goes, and the upper aileron on
     that side **floats hinge-moment-free** (H = a + b·δ = 0 on its own strips: trailing edge up ~α/3 in level flight),
     off the stick; the other side works. **Great Lakes:** the flight config has aileron rows on the LOWER wing only (the
     own model has four ailerons and slave struts), so a lower-panel loss takes that side's only aileron and roll power
     halves. **Add upper aileron rows to the GL config?** That changes its roll rate and needs a re-rig — not done here.
     Single-aileron monoplanes lose the aileron on the panel that went; the other still works.
  8. **Prop strike:** the disc does not push (a turning blade cuts or curls); the ground drags the tips round with μ·N·R
     against the engine's P/ω and the rotor's inertia. A 5 mm brush curls the tips by what went in (thrust at the same
     power ∝ R^(2/3)) and the engine **runs on**; a nose-over brakes it under a quarter of idle in a fraction of a second
     — **sudden stoppage**. A blade in the water stops it outright.
  9. **Sound/dust hooks:** `Aircraft.Contact` (ScrapeStart/Stop with surface and μ·N·v in W, PanelBent, PanelBroken,
     PropStrike, PropStoppage, each with world position/velocity) and `Aircraft.Scrapes` per frame. Placeholder noise and
     dust are in (`ContactEffects`); the real ones are Codex's (next item).

      only? **ANSWERED (Ty, 2026-11-03): static load counts** — kept, verified and tested in lane/claude-crash-physics

    start (turbulence is a frozen field). The difference came from the Unity side, and there were two faults:
    1. **The first frame of a new flight flew the LAST flight's stick and power.** `ResetFlight` rebuilt the
       aeroplane but left the driver's inputs alone; the controls stop publishing while the menu is open, and
       nothing orders the two `Update`s, so the long first frame (0.05 s, ten sim steps) flew whatever the stick
       was doing when you opened the menu (on a cold start: 50 % power, elevator off trim, held). Measured on the
       Pitts: 0.05 s of full left stick turns a +20.6° RIGHT bank at 60 s into −12.5° LEFT (stick-fixed), −24° (free).
       **Now every start seeds the inputs on its own hands-off trim.**

       the 8BitDo connected their bars are hidden. 5 % of left aileron trim: −50° of bank in 10 s. **Now centred
       on every new flight**, as the pitch trim already was.

    the 4,000 ft rig over-correcting lower down plus the spiral, and it is the SAME every launch. A LEFT turn there
    came from the first moments of the flight. Stick-free makes the spiral much faster (the same 0.05 s nudge at the

- **SIDE-BY-SIDE VR FOR A CARDBOARD HEADSET (Claude, 2026-11-01, lane/claude-vr-stereo) — engine and app logic
  only; the lenses are Codex's. NEEDS YOU on a real headset, five things:**
  1. **IPD.** It ships at **63 mm** with a slider from 55 to 75 in Options → Controls. 63 mm is the adult mean,
     not a measurement of you. If the two images will not fuse, or you get eye strain after a few minutes, that
     slider is the first thing to move — tell me the number that works and I will make it the default.
  2. **Does the lens profile match YOUR viewer?** `configs/vr-cardboard.json` holds Google's published **Cardboard
     v2** profile verbatim (inter-lens 63.9 mm, screen-to-lens 39.3 mm, tray-to-lens 35 mm, k1 0.33582564,
     k2 0.55348791, 60° each way, bottom-aligned), because you said generic. If your headset is something else,
     its own profile goes in that file and nothing in code changes. A wrong profile shows up as the picture
     bowing at the edges or the two halves not sitting where your eyes are.
  3. **The recentre gesture.** Recentre is **touch and hold anywhere for 0.6 s**, plus a button in Options and an
     automatic recentre every time VR is switched on. With the phone in a headset you cannot see the screen, so
     this is the one control you have to find blind through the case's opening — if your headset has no
     opening, or 0.6 s is too easy to trigger by accident while the phone seats, say so.
  4. **How do you fly it?** VR hides every touch overlay — the stick, the hat, the throttle, the HUD — because
     you cannot see them and a stray thumb would move the controls. **So there is NO touch control in VR: you
     need a gamepad**, which is left enabled. I have not flown it that way. If you want to go up in VR without a
     gamepad, that is a real design question and it is yours, not mine: tell me what you would reach for.
  5. **Comfort, which is the one thing no test here can see.** Head tracking is **one for one** (gain 1,
     deliberately NOT the look-gain slider, which stays yours to set for the mono view) so the world stays put
     when you move your head, which is what stops people feeling ill. If it feels like it lags, or swims, or the
     horizon tips when you turn your head, stop and tell me — that is not something to push through.
  **Assumptions I made, each of which you can overrule:** 63 mm IPD; Cardboard v2 as the generic profile; render
  scale **0.85** (sharpness against frame rate on a phone that is now drawing the world twice); a **40°** roll
  limit, which is not from a document — yaw and pitch reuse the neck limits the mono look already had, and
  nothing had ever limited roll, so I picked a number a neck can actually do and it is a guess; landscape lock
  and the sleep timeout are forced while VR is on and restored on exit. **No new SDK**: Google's Cardboard XR
  plugin would have brought a whole XR stack in to do what 200 lines of frustum maths does, and it does not
  know about the authored seat eyes. **VR supersedes the mono device-look while it is on** — `CockpitView` skips
  its own gyro path — and turning VR off puts the mono view back exactly as it was; the
  lane/claude-look-default 3.5 gain is untouched.

  2. **Blanketing: you were right for your build.** island-nav's single-wing wake holds the stab at 0.495 of free-stream q
     from α 30 to 45. This lane's per-section wakes put the lower wing's wake above the stab past ~18°: q 1.00 at 30–75°.
  3. **"Elevator weak at high α" — found and fixed, fleet-wide (32 tail tables).** The 2-D→3-D tail rescale stretched the
     whole α axis, so broadside the stab read its section at ~51°: lift 0.95 where a plate has 0, normal force flat at
     0.83. Elevator authority (full up − full down) at α 45 was **0.00** of its α 0 value; now **0.21**. Each point now
     moves by its own lift's induced angle (NACA Report 865) — the same as before in the linear range.
  4. **Inverted, full power, right rudder (+ right aileron): reproduced — it rolls out.** It flattens to −86°, the wings
     bank, and the propeller's gyroscopic YAW (h·q, which appears as soon as the wings bank) stops the yaw: r 138 → −10
     deg/s, β → 81°, and it rolls through knife-edge into an upright spin every ~20 s. Same with aileron neutral (15 s)
     and faster with right aileron (9 s). With the gyro switched off the inverted spin is steady but steep (−32°), so the
     gyro both MAKES the inverted flat and ENDS it. Gyro formula checked (H×ω), inertia is your 80-lb Hartzell figure.
     **Not fixed: I have not found the physics that holds a real one there, and I will not tune it in.** Regression test
     written and SKIPPED as OPEN (`PittsPowerSpinTargetTests`).

     5 decimals from 0 to 120° (one section alone: ≤ 0.0001, the 0.37° rig offset). Every term on the path uses |α| or the
     section's own negative stall. Table in the Log.
  6. **Aileron power IN spins is down a lot from your build** (run #2's aileron sections): ΔC_l in the developed spin

- **ROLL RATE, WHOLE FLEET + PITTS SPIN/BREAK-UP — PLEASE FLY (Claude, 2026-11-02, lane/claude-pitts-spin, runs #1 and #2).
  Not merged, not installed.**
  1. **Rolls at 160 mph IAS, full aileron, rudder centred.** The Pitts now rolls **~206–218 deg/s** against your
     225 (−3 to −9 %, depending on whether the speed gained in the roll is counted). Nothing was tuned to reach it.
     Every aeroplane rolls 15–42 % slower than before. C172 at 110 mph: 73. J-3 at 75 mph: 47. P-51 at 250 mph: 121.
     Fleet table in the Log. **Fly a few rolls in the Pitts, the 172 and the Cub, and tell me the rate AND how
     quickly it gets there.**
  2. **What was wrong** applied to every aeroplane. The hinged aileron row was flown as its own aerofoil at α + δ,
     so at full travel it was stalled. The roll itself then un-stalled it, so the aileron got 24 % stronger once the
     roll was under way. Each aileron section now shifts its lift by τ(E)·η_δ(E, δ)·δ:
     - τ from Glauert, using that section's own measured chord ratio;
     - η_δ from Torenbeek's sealed-gap plain-flap data (Olson, NASA NTRS 20150006019, Fig. 3a).
  3. **Biplane interference (Munk/Prandtl) is in, and it does NOT slow the roll.** It is computed for each cellule
     with a vortex lattice built from that aeroplane's own wing strips. It takes about 15 % out of BOTH the aileron
     moment and the roll damping, so the Pitts' rate goes +4 %. The Great Lakes and Stearman go +6–11 %, because
     their ailerons are on one wing only. It is exactly zero on monoplanes.
  4. **OPEN — the Extra is now LOW: 224–239 deg/s at 160 mph** against your ~340–400. Three possible reasons:
     - its 30° aileron travel is deep in the plain-flap fall-off (η_δ ≈ 0.50);
     - its spades add some lift and are not modelled, because there is no geometry source;
     - the published number's speed is unknown.
     **At what speed does a 300 do 400 deg/s?**
  5. **OPEN — hinge gap.** η_δ is SEALED-gap data. In flight, NACA TN 632 (Fairchild 22) found that sealing the gap
     bought about +20–33 % effectiveness. **Are the Pitts' aileron gaps sealed?** If not, physics says the Pitts is
     nearer ~170–180, which is Aviat's figure, and that may be where Aviat's ~180 comes from. Nothing has been
     applied without a measured gap.
  6. **OPEN — roll onset may be too crisp.** Lifting-surface theory says the model's roll DAMPING is 1.5–2.6 times
     too high. The steady rate is right to within −8..+3 % on monoplanes; the Pitts is +9 %, which would take it to
     about 225. Over-damping makes the time to reach the rate too short (Pitts 0.30 s to 90 %). Correcting it
     fleet-wide is a separate change, and it touches spins. **Does the Pitts reach its rate too abruptly?**
  7. **OPEN — Great Lakes: does yours have ailerons on all four wings?** The config has lower ailerons only, while
     the model has had upper ailerons since v11. Lower-only gives 71 deg/s at 160 mph.
  8. **Spins (run #1's tail wakes; unchanged by run #2), 45 s, full aft, full rudder, Pitts.** Turn time / alpha:
     | power | rudder | before run #1 | after run #1 | now |
     |---|---|---|---|---|
     | idle | left | 3.93 s, α 35° | 2.02 s, α 32° | 2.02 s, α 32° |
     | idle | right | 2.39 s, α 31° | 1.50 s, α 31° | 1.50 s, α 31° |
     | ~40 % | left | 2.30 s, α 90° FLAT | 2.16 s, α 90° FLAT | 2.16 s, α 90° FLAT |
     | ~40 % | right | 1.77 s, α 29° | 1.16 s, α 31° | 1.15 s, α 31° |
     | full | left | 2.71 s, α 117° FLAT | 3.01 s, α 97° FLAT | 3.01 s, α 97° FLAT |
     | full | right | 1.12 s, α 30° | 0.91 s, α 30° | 0.91 s, α 30° |

     Idle spins are steep and faster both ways. **Power-on LEFT spins still go flat**: that is the prop's gyroscopic
     couple (`TailWakeTests` shows they are not flat without it). Is that what a real S-2B does with power left in
     a left spin?
  9. **Wing break-up:** the left ailerons and the left aileron strut now leave with the left wing (they used to stay
     on the fuselage). Check it in a g-overload.
  10. **Rigs re-solved:** aileron rigs are 8–10 % larger, the Pitts' 35 % larger; the rest is in docs/RIGGING.md.

  - **What a rig is now:** two fixed angles in each config's new `rig` block, built into the airframe: the ailerons'

    leading edge LEFT). The elevator is not rigged; its hands-off value is the TRIM, and the air start sets the slider

    own forces: prop torque, P-factor, spiral slipstream, the slipstream swirl over the stab and the thrust line,
    lifted out of `Aircraft` so the two cannot differ. Unknowns: airspeed, α, elevator, aileron rig, fin offset and
    bank, stick and rudder centred, zero sideslip, LEVEL, at 75 % of rated power (the engine model's own definition:
    power = MaxPowerW × throttle, no altitude lapse), 4,000 ft ISA. Gliders: best glide from the model's own polar.
    All 34 converge to residual < 2e-12 of the weight. `RigTool` (`RIG_WRITE=1`) wrote them; no fudge factors.

- **CRASH IN WATER — PHYSICS LANE (Claude, 2026-11-02, lane/claude-crash-water). Silent until the audio lane merges.**
  `StructuralDamage` no longer calls `_audio.Crash` at all. Every crash impact now goes out as a `CrashEvents`
  impact with Land or Water, and lane/codex-crash-audio's FlightAudio is what has to play it. **Merge the two lanes
  together, or crashes make no sound.** The probe and its numbers are in
  `~/Developer/agent-lanes/aero-playground/crash-water/probe.txt` (and `.csv`). Decisions for you:
  1. **Water does not break a 172 that land does.** I used the same arrival for both: 30 m/s along, 20 m/s down,
     30° nose-down. On land the 172 breaks into 7 pieces. In water it stays in one piece and floats. Each hard
     point is judged by its closing speed at first touch, and the water's added mass (von Kármán slam) takes the
     speed off before the cabin points get there: 6–7 m/s against the 8 m/s cabin break. What should break an
     airframe in water is the slam LOAD. That needs a new break criterion, and I have not invented one. The probe's
     third case forces the break-up at first water contact so you can see the pieces: nose, tail boom, both wings.
  2. **The remnant keeps the mass of what it lost.** The rule is yours: `LoseComponent` leaves mass alone, and
     `AirframeContactTests` pins it. So a cabin that has lost its engine and wings is still 1,043 kg and sinks in
     0.8 s. Its own parts would float it. I wrote mass shedding, broke that test, and took it out again. Your call
     whether the rule stands now that every lost piece is simulated as its own body.
  3. **Unmeasured openings, marked ASSUMED in `Core/Wreck/WaterPhysics.cs`.** Each one is a real dimension:
     - door-seal gap: 1 mm around two 0.96 m doors, 77 cm² in all
     - drain holes: 1/4 in, one per 0.4 m rib bay
     - cowl inlets and exit: 0.06 m² each
     - fuel vent and feed lines: 3/8 in
     - engine taken as half aluminium, half steel: 4,100 kg/m³

     Intact ditching time is set almost entirely by the door seals. Measure one 172 door gap and the number
     becomes real.
  4. **Fast ditching.** 24 m/s with the gear down: the wheels dig in (existing `WheelHydro`), it noses over to
     −38° and recovers. It stays intact apart from the prop. I expected a harder flip.
  5. **Floating bodies bob for a long time.** Wave-radiation damping is not modelled, only drag.
  - **Probe highlights** (C172 at reference load: 2 × 40 kg fuel, 86 kg pilot).
    - Pieces. Masses come from Raymer's GA weight buildup, scaled to the config's 877 kg empty mass.
      - Engine+cowl (240 kg): sinks at once and never resurfaces. Reserve gone at 0.9 s; on a 10 m bed at 7 s.
      - Each wing (156 kg, sealed tank inside): resurfaces at 1.3 s, floats, sinks at 340 s, on the bed at 351 s.
      - Tail boom (135 kg): floats, sinks at 312 s.
      - Gear legs: straight down.
    - Intact ditching (12 m/s, nose-up 8°): still afloat at 30 min, nose-down 22°, 2.9 m³ of water in, air
      escaping at 0.1 L/s.
    - Undamaged floats: 0 kg of water in 15 min.
    - Left float holed in all four compartments (rock + pump-out cap off): lists −27° at 5 min, capsizes left by
      20 min. Lessons can do this through `PracticeScenario.FloatDamage`.

    Bridge offline against Unity 6000.3's iOS managed DLLs (C# 9, netstandard2.1): 0 errors. No gate is marked

- **GREAT LAKES FRONT PANEL, SECOND PASS — YOUR TWO FAULTS, AND A THIRD UNDER ONE OF THEM (Claude, 2026-11-01,
  lane/claude-gl-dials):**
  1. **The compass is a box with a window in it now.** You were right that the card hung out in the open and
     that Codex's case face was nowhere to be seen — and the cause was that I had built the thing inside out.
     The pilot sits at smaller x; the card drum's near face was 29 mm NEARER you than the face plate, so the
     drum was outside the case and the plate was buried behind it. From you outwards it now goes: the alpha
     face plate (aft-most, 2 mm proud), then the case, then the card wholly inside it. The case is **five walls
     with the aft side open** — a solid box would have hidden the very card the window exists to show — and it
     is 62 mm deep, because a 53 mm card has to fit in there, which is about how deep a real wet compass is.
     Measured off the export: the drum clears the case by 2.9 mm forward, 5.6 mm aft, 5.3 mm each side and
     9.6 mm above and below, and the face plate is unobstructed from the front eye at 25 of 25 sample points,
     so the lubber line is in view.
  2. **The chrome bezel was never broken. Its neighbours were eating it.** I measured the ring first: 384
     triangles, all 360 degrees covered, no hole — one step from telling you it was just reflection. It was the
     **tachometer's face cutting into it**. Every adjacent pair in that row of six interpenetrated, by 8 to
     16 mm; the five dark bezels had the same fault and hid it, because a dark ring cut by a dark face still
     looks like a dark ring. **My doing, last commit**: I scaled the audit's photo spacing down to the row's
     existing 290 mm width, and six real instruments do not fit in 290 mm.
  3. **So the row is spaced properly now, and that is the part worth your eye.** Sizes are real instrument
     cases — three 3-1/8 in (altimeter, ASI, tachometer) and three 2-1/4 in — and the photo's own numbers are
     what argue for it: the three small ones measure 0.71, 0.70 and 0.67 of the ASI, all within a millimetre of
     a 2-1/4 in case, and the large ones read 1.10 and 0.90 because the altimeter is nearest your oblique
     camera and the tachometer furthest. Spacing is the audit's ratios taken **as metres** — one ASI diameter
     per unit — giving a **477 mm row on a 724 mm panel**, with 12.9 mm of air at the tightest pair and 40 mm
     at the widest. The panel's toggle switch moved up beside the warning lamp, because the altimeter now
     occupies where it used to sit. **Does that row match your photograph?** It is wider than before and the
     tachometer has moved outboard.
  4. **I lit the compass card, and you should say whether you want that.** Once the card was inside a closed
     case it went dark: at 000 the render read a bare N where it had read 3 N 33 out in the open. A real
     whiskey compass carries its own lamp, so the card material is now self-lit (emissive at 0.6). It is the
     only self-lit thing on the aeroplane apart from the avionics displays. If you would rather it were lit by
     the cockpit like everything else and simply dim, say so and it comes straight back out.
  5. **Codex's band art and his face art disagree, and I cannot settle it from here — ART, NEEDS YOU.** At 000
     the card reads **N** under the lubber line and at 090 it reads **E**, so the sign is right. But only the
     letter under the line is legible: the numbers either side compress away. The audit's band contract says
     the window shows **66.8 degrees** of card, which is a FLAT strip read through a slot. The card in the
     model is a drum, and the 360-degree band has to wrap its circumference, because one degree of heading must
     be one degree of card. The window is 53.3 mm and the drum is 53.3 mm across — so the window spans **180
     degrees** of it, and everything but the middle is squeezed into the silhouette. To show 66.8 degrees the
     drum would have to be **96.8 mm across, in a case about 105 mm wide**, and the face art draws a 64 mm
     housing. So either the compass gets bigger (and Codex redraws the face), or the band is redrawn for a
     cylindrical card. Not mine to pick — it is his art and your panel.

- **PITTS ROLL RATE, third time — the 0.66 is GONE and the cause was geometry (Claude, 2026-11-01,
  lane/claude-pitts-roll) — PLEASE FLY IT, and three open questions:**
  1. **You were right about the double-count, and the "corroboration" I offered was circular.** τ is already in
     the model as the fixed row's camber gain `g = 0.85·τ(E)` (docs/CONTROL-SURFACES.md). The thin-aerofoil
     τ ≈ 0.60 I cited as independent confirmation of 0.66 was the model's own assumption handed back to me.
     `effectiveness` is removed from both copies of the Pitts config; the field stays as a documented hook at
     1.0, used by no aircraft, and is explicitly **not** τ. The travel stays on TCDS A8SO 25°.
  2. **What was actually wrong: camber applied past the end of the aileron.** A deflection cambers the fixed
     strip ahead of it, and that was being applied across the strip's WHOLE span even where the aileron had
     already ended — roll power with no roll damping to go with it, which lands straight on the steady rate.
     Coverage is **1.000 for 28 of the fleet's 32 aileron and elevator systems and they are bit-for-bit
     unchanged**; it is wrong only on the four surfaces rebuilt from their GLB models on 2026-10-28 (Pitts
     upper 0.681, lower 0.719, Extra 0.826, Great Lakes 0.877). Nothing was tuned.
  3. **Roll rate at 160 mph IAS, full aileron** — before (physics, no 0.66) → after, with the per-fix split:

     | aircraft | before | SHIPPED (+coverage) | (wing rescale, not shipped) | real | to 90 % |
     |---|---|---|---|---|---|
     | Pitts S-2B | 391.6 | **291.1** | 311.4 | yours 260–300 (Aviat ~180) | 0.41 → 0.35 s |
     | Extra 300 | 409.3 | **362.2** | 364.1 | ~400 | 0.30 s |
     | Great Lakes | 83.3 | **77.2** | 80.7 | — | 0.18 s |
     | C172 (110 mph) | 127.5 | **127.5** | 127.5 | — | 1.14 s |
     | J-3 Cub (75 mph) | 79.6 | **79.6** | 79.6 | — | 1.78 s |
     | 2-33 (60 mph) | 28.4 | **28.4** | 28.4 | — | 0.14 s |

     **The Pitts lands at 291 deg/s, inside your 260–300, from the geometry fix alone with nothing tuned.**

  4. **OPEN — the Pitts is ~4 % above the top of your band and the Extra is ~9 % BELOW its ~400.** I have not
     touched either. The Extra moved the wrong way when the geometry was fixed, which makes me suspect its
     0.826 coverage is partly a measurement artefact of its GLB rather than real. **Does an Extra 300 really
     out-roll a Pitts S-2B, and by how much?** Your answer decides whether the Extra's aileron geometry needs
     re-measuring.
  5. **OPEN — the Aviat ~180 deg/s figure contradicts your 260–300.** I have used yours. If Aviat's is a
     different condition (a lower speed, a half-deflection, an S-2C) it would be worth knowing which.
  6. **OPEN — the model over-saturates the ailerons by 18 % and I left it.** You asked for DATCOM large-
     deflection saturation; it is already there and already stronger than DATCOM. The hinged strip samples its
     section table at α + δ, which at 25° is past the stall, giving effectiveness **0.63 against DATCOM's
     0.75**. Adding a `tanh` would have made it ~0.47 — the same double-count as the 0.66. Forcing it UP to the
     DATCOM curve instead would put the Pitts at ~369, above your band, so something else is also off
     (Munk biplane interference is not modelled; the Pitts' own section table is a candidate). Two errors are
     currently pointing opposite ways and I would rather say so than let the total look right.
  7. **Not done, with reasons.** No hinge-gap/flex loss: a ~0.9 is real physics but nothing in any config
     records whether a gap is sealed, so the number would be chosen rather than derived. No Extra spade
     geometry: they are stick-force devices (neutral, they lie along the airstream and do nothing), no public
     source gives their chord/span/area, and the effect is already carried where it belongs — the Extra's
     aileron has the BALANCED hinge coefficients −0.10/−0.30 against a plain surface's −0.20/−0.45.
  8. **OPEN, and the one I want your steer on — the wing finite-span rescale is BUILT, MEASURED and NOT
     SHIPPED.** You were right that nine wing surfaces carry 2-D slopes with no finite-span correction (Pitts
     6.30, Great Lakes 6.17, Extra / Cassutt / Swift / drone 5.82, 737 5.53) and that the tails have had the
     Helmbold rescale since 2026-10-06. I applied it, measured it, and took it back out, because it makes the
     aeroplanes fly worse:

     | | lift-off as shipped | with the rescale | real |
     |---|---|---|---|
     | Pitts S-2B | 34.0 m/s (76 mph) | 40.2 m/s (90 mph) | ~60–70 mph |
     | Extra 300 | 38.7 m/s (87 mph) | 44.7 m/s (100 mph) | ~60–70 mph |

     Helmbold keeps CLmax and moves the stall to a higher incidence, and a taildragger is pinned at its ground
     attitude, so it simply needs more speed. That is an 18 % error on a book-checked number, bought for 7 %
     on the roll rate — in the wrong direction there too. **The slope is still wrong**; what the measurement
     says is that these wings' area, incidence and CLmax were authored against the 2-D slope and absorb it, so
     the wing has to be re-derived as a whole rather than the table corrected under it. Say the word and it is
     its own lane. `TheseWingsStillCarryTwoDimensionalSectionTables` keeps the list so it cannot be lost.
  9. **Fleet effect of what DID ship**: four glide-table rows moved (Pitts, Extra, Great Lakes, Jenny — the

     glide ratio 5.697 → 5.695). Everything else is bit-for-bit unchanged, protected by a 1 % deadband on the

- **DEVICE LOOK-AROUND: THE AXES WERE NEVER RESOLVED AGAINST THE WORLD (Claude, 2026-11-01, lane/claude-device-look)
  — fixed, NEEDS YOU to re-fly it:**
  1. **What you flew on 2026.1101.0549 and what was wrong.** You reported three things — turning and rolling the
     phone did the same thing, neither moved the view purely (everything came out diagonal), and tilting did
     nothing. All three are one bug. `CockpitLook.FromDevice` took `reference⁻¹ · current` and read yaw and pitch
     off that quaternion's components. **That delta is expressed in the phone's OWN axes**, so which component a
     movement landed in depended entirely on how you happened to be holding the phone when it zeroed: from any
     natural pose one physical rotation spilled into two components at once (diagonal), two different rotations
     landed on overlapping components (turn ≡ roll), and the third landed on the roll component, which was thrown
     away (pitch ignored). It was **not** a handedness bug and **not** a screen-orientation bug — no axis swap
     fixes a frame that moves with the sensor.
  2. **What it does now.** It follows where the phone is AIMED — the back of the device, its local −z — and
     resolves that against world vertical: yaw is the change in the aim's bearing about world up, pitch the change
     in its elevation above the horizon. The three come out independent by construction, and **rolling the phone
     does not move the aim at all**, so it does nothing — which is also why **portrait and landscape need no
     special case**: holding the phone the other way up IS a roll about the aim. No Unity-side change was needed;
     the bug was entirely in the Core arithmetic, and `Input.gyro.attitude`'s raw CoreMotion numbers are exactly
     what that arithmetic wants.
  3. **Please re-fly it and say whether 1× is right.** Turn the phone about the vertical → view pans left/right;
     tilt it toward or away → view pitches up/down; roll it → nothing. Each pure. RECENTRE under the look pad
     zeroes it wherever you are holding it. **One assumption I could not test from here**: that the attitude
     frame's vertical is its +z, which is what CoreMotion documents and what Unity passes through. If pitch and
     yaw come out swapped, that is the assumption — `CockpitLook.BackOf` and `ViewDeltaOf` are the only two
     places it lives, and the symptom would be a clean swap, not the mush you flew.
  4. **The old tests all passed while it was broken**, because every one of them zeroed from a tidy pose.
     `FromAnyPoseAMovementIsStillPure` zeroes from turned-37 tilted-23 rolled-61 and is the test that would have
     caught this on the bench. 62 tests in `CockpitLookTests` now, including pure yaw / pure pitch / inert roll in
     portrait, both landscapes and upside down, fed as raw CoreMotion-style attitudes.

- **MOVE THE DEVICE TO LOOK AROUND (Claude, 2026-11-01, lane/claude-device-look) — NEEDS YOU, three things:**
  1. **It is on a slider and the default is 1×, which is the one worth flying first.** Options → "Move the
     device to look around (cockpit view)", then "Look gain 1.0× (1° of device = 1.0° of view)", continuous to
     10×. 1× reads as a window: the phone is a hole in the canopy. Above about 3× it stops being a window and
     becomes a control — useful for finding the runway on base without turning your whole body, but the horizon
     no longer sits still. **Which gain feels right is yours**; the slider is there so you can land on it in the
     air rather than me guessing a number.
  2. **The look pad did NOT work while the old "goggles" option was on**, and nothing said so — `CockpitView`
     returned out of the frame before the hat ran, so switching the option on silently removed the on-screen
     arrows. They compose now: `CockpitLook` keeps the hat's offset and the device's apart and clamps only the
     sum, so a snap over the shoulder plus a lean of the phone add up, and letting go of the pad no longer
     snatches the view back from where you are holding the device. RECENTRE sits under the pad and zeroes both
     against however you are holding it at that moment.
  3. **There is no tilt steering in the game, so nothing double-counts — today.** `Input.gyro`,
     `Input.acceleration` and the InputSystem sensors appear in `CockpitView.cs` and nowhere else; tilting the
     phone moves the view and only the view. If tilt steering is ever added it must take its OWN reference and
     its own zero, because feeding one attitude to both would make looking out of the left window roll the
     aeroplane left. That is written at the point where the gyro is switched on, where whoever adds it will be
     standing.
  Limits unchanged and still enforced on the SUM: 160° of yaw, 75° up, 60° down. At 10× that is reached after
  16° of device, and turning back brings the view straight back rather than unwinding stored offset, which is
  asserted. Not VR: this is one eye, not stereo — the seat eye points are the basis for that when it comes.

- **THE EXTRA'S PROPELLER TURNS (Claude, 2026-11-01, lane/claude-prop-spin) — NEEDS YOU, two things, and one
  correction to what I told you earlier:**
  1. **Fixed, and it was only the Extra.** A model with its own rig skips the hinge carve — correctly, carving a
     rigged model tears the draughtsman's parts — but the carve is ALSO where a model's propeller is handed to
     the turning hub. So `SpinProps` turned a hub with nothing on it while the blades stood still, and the
     procedural blades that would have turned were hidden with the rest of the procedural shell.
     `AirframeBuilder.BindModelProp` now re-parents the model's `Prop` and `Spinner` nodes onto the hub, centred
     on the spinner, with the blades on their own bone so the blur disc can still take over above ~350 rpm.
     **I told you earlier that the Pitts and the Great Lakes were static too. They are not.** Neither of their
     rigs binds, so both go down the carve path and both propellers were already turning — the carve skins the
     blades to the hub's bones, which is why the node's transform never moves and why the first version of this
     check reported four false failures. `PropSpinCheck` knows the difference now.
  2. **The Great Lakes' rig is dead and says nothing about it.** `docs/models/great-lakes-own-rig.json` names 58
     nodes and **all 58 are missing from `great-lakes-like-own.glb`** — it was written for a cockpit that never
     shipped in that GLB. `AirframeRig.Bind` returns null when NOTHING binds and logs only when something does,
     so a rig that matches nothing is completely silent. The aeroplane flies (the carve picks up the surfaces and
     the propeller), but none of its instruments move and nobody would know. Two separate calls for you: whether
     the Great Lakes should get its cockpit GLB rebuilt to match the rig, and whether `Bind` should shout when it
     binds zero of N.
  3. **The 172's and the J-3's propellers really are static**, for a different reason: the carve cannot separate
     the propeller from those downloaded meshes, and `AirframeVisual` deliberately handles that by keeping the
     model's own blades and suppressing the blur disc. `PropSpinCheck` reports it rather than failing, because
     fixing it means re-cutting someone else's mesh. Your call whether that is worth a lane.

- **WHY IT OPENED AND STILL WOULD NOT FLY: the view and the controls were one bug, and it was neither (Claude, 2026-10-31). FIXED.** Codex's `e2f4fd6` made the world affordable (70.4 -> 0.78 us a sample) and Ty installed it at 05:40 PDT: it plays. It then showed two faults — the camera far away with the aeroplane a tiny speck below it, and controls that did nothing. **One cause, and it is not the camera rig and not the input binding.** `WorldTerrain.Airports` reads the island's eight airports, but `WorldTerrain.AirportStrips` was still the four-airport world's template — one 2,400 m runway along +x at every field, with a crosswind runway along +y — and `ChooseRunway` was applying it to the island's airport centres. Every start therefore sat 1,570 m off the field on a heading of 000, on ground that has nothing to do with the pad:

  | field | template start | island ground there | field elevation | out by |
  |---|---|---|---|---|
  | PHDH | (4330, 4990) | 789.1 m | 4.3 m | **785 m underground** |
  | PATK | (3420, -6340) | 906.8 m | 111.3 m | **795 m underground** |
  | 3U2 | (-2330, 1820) | 1363.7 m | 1511.8 m | 148 m in the air |
  | KMYL | (1210, -880) | 394.6 m | 1531.3 m | **1,137 m in the air** |
  | KMEV | (-3300, -3020) | 1402.1 m | 1439.9 m | 38 m in the air |
  | PANC / KPGA / KSNA | — | — | — | 30 m, 24 m up; KSNA 7 m under |

  PHDH is `DefaultAirportIndex`, so the FLY button's own default start was 785 m inside a hillside. **An aeroplane under the ground reaches `Math.Sign(NaN)` in `LandingGear.Compute` (LandingGear.cs:428) and throws `ArithmeticException` on its FIRST step** — reproduced in a probe, stack trace and all. `FlightSimDriver.Update` has no catch, so `ApplyStateToTransform()` never runs: the airframe never moves and nothing the pilot does reaches the sim. Meanwhile `ChaseCamera.KeepAboveSurface` — which by owner rule may never go below the ground — lifts the camera to 790 m every frame and re-aims it down at an aeroplane 785 m below. **That is the wrong view and the dead controls, both of them, from the one spawn.** Ty's `AERO_SELFTEST=perf` run was clean because the perf test flies and never sat on that runway.
  **The fix, consuming Codex's geometry and changing none of it.** New `src/FlyingGame.Core/IslandRunways.cs` (mine) serves the island's own runways as the `RunwayEnd` the spawn, tow, approach and practice paths already speak, read straight from `IslandField` — real centre, real true heading, real length, real surface, real slope — and chooses an end by headwind for arbitrary true headings, the crosswind choice being a runway on a genuinely different axis (KMEV 17/35 vs 13/31) rather than the other end of the same one (KSNA 2L and 2R are parallel and are not a crosswind choice). `WorldTerrain.ChooseRunway` delegates to it when a world is installed and keeps the old template as `ChooseTemplateRunway` for the widget and the flat-ground tests — that is the only edit to `WorldTerrain.cs`, three lines and a comment, and no airport, runway, pad or elevation was touched. `FlightSimDriver.Spawn` now takes its pad elevation from the ground at the start point rather than a field-wide figure (3U2 slopes 0.5 %, Cabin Creek 3 %), and in free flight takes its airborne start from `IslandSites.Starts` — the world's own authored position, true heading and altitude — instead of deriving one, because a derived start has no way to know the ground 600 m off KMEV's runway is 1,100 m lower. Events keep their own starts.
  **What says it works.** `TheRunwayChoiceAgreesWithTheStartTheWorldAuthored`: in calm air the end my chooser picks matches Codex's authored `OnTheRunway` start **to 0.1 m and 0.1 degrees at all eight airports** — the world and the sim now agree about where a flight begins, which is the real proof that this reads the island rather than guessing at it. `EveryAirportStartsOnItsOwnRunway` holds the start on a runway of that field, on ground within 1 m of the strip's own plane, across 8 wind directions x headwind/crosswind x calm/breeze. `NoStartPutsAnAeroplaneInsideTheGround` holds the 172 and the Cub on their wheels (CG 0.2-6 m above the pad) and both the on-final and airborne starts clear. `TheControlsMoveTheAeroplaneAtEveryStart` is the direct regression for the dead controls: full throttle for 15 s rolls the 172 **220-260 m and reaches 28-30 m/s at every one of the eight airports**, and asserts no NaN. New `AERO_SELFTEST=starts` walks all eight airports x six start modes on the device and reports, per start, the height above ground, where the camera ended up relative to the aeroplane, Unity errors thrown, and how far the aeroplane moves when the controls are pushed.

  floats launched frozen: 12 ft, 10 kt, alpha 180, beta +90, nothing on the pads moving it. Those are not flight
  values, they are the spawn, frozen — and every one of them is arithmetic. `WorldTerrain.Lakes` is the
  four-airport world's water the way `AirportStrips` was its land: one lake 3 km south-west of every field at the

  the Cub's float keel (1.55) less its resting draft (0.25); 10 kt is the 5 m/s session wind; beta 90 is that
  wind from the east on an aeroplane heading north; alpha 180 is what is left when there is no forward airspeed
  at all. The state never advanced because the first step went to NaN, 448 m inside a hill.

  field's own height that is long enough for the hull. It now picks what a pilot would — PANC gets **Lake Hood**
  1.3 km away, KMYL **Payette Lake** 1.2 km (McCall really is on it), KPGA **Lake Powell**, PATK the AP8 float
  pond, and the coastal fields the sea 2 km out. Nearest-by-distance alone was not enough: it sent PHDH's Cub,
  which lives at 4 m by the sea, to an alpine tarn 2,030 m up a mountain because it was 3 km closer, so the
  choice weights every metre of climb as ten metres of travel. Flying boats need 2.2 km and no authored lake has
  it, so the H-4 goes to sea, found by walking outward from the field until there is a clear run — not by me
  inventing a harbour, because the coast is Codex's. `EverySeaplaneStartsOnWaterDeepEnoughToFloat` holds it for
  the J-3, PA-18 and Beaver on floats and the H-4, at all eight fields: water present, bed below it, long enough,
  and the resting spawn above the bed.

  floatplane too (96 starts, not 48), and it survives a start that throws instead of dying on the first one — the
  thing built to find bad starts was being stopped by the first bad start.
- **WHAT THE PITTS "FREEZE" ACTUALLY IS: low-altitude flight costs 13 fps, and the water query is why (Claude,
  2026-10-31). NOT FIXED — the expensive part is Codex's, handed off below.** Ty: "I was not underwater when it
  froze I was flying around at ~3,000 ft." He was right and my first answer was wrong. Reproduced on the iPad
  with `AERO_SELFTEST=cruise`, a Pitts holding altitude for three minutes:
  `t=0s 61 fps agl 412` ... `t=30s **13 fps** agl 10` ... `t=36s **13 fps** agl 19` ... `t=42s 17 fps agl 1`.
  **At 412 m above the ground it runs at 61 fps; at 10-20 m above the ground it runs at 13.** Nothing else
  changed — same aeroplane, same flight, no errors, heap flat at 33-36 MB. And note what "3,000 ft" means on this
  island: the inland fields are at 1,500 m (4,900 ft), so 3,000 ft on the altimeter over the plateau is BELOW the
  terrain tops, in a valley, at low AGL. His cruise was a low-level cruise whether or not he meant it to be.
  Measured per query, on this machine: `GroundHeightAt` **3.6-4.2 us** (Codex's index, working), but
  `FloatHydro.WaterSurfaceAt` **7.5 us over the sea and 14.4 us at KSNA**, and `WheelGroundHeightAt` 4.4-9.6 us.
  The contact solver asks for all of them for every contact point at every RK4 stage: 15 points x 4 stages x
  200 Hz is 12,000 of each per second of flight, and the altitude gate I added only closes above 60 m AGL, which
  is exactly where the frame rate is fine anyway. Below it, the water query alone is 90-170 ms of CPU per second.
- **[Claude -> codex] HANDOFF: `IslandTerrain.WaterAt` never got the treatment `HeightKm` did, and it is now the
  most expensive thing in low-level flight** (src/FlyingGame.Core/IslandTerrain.cs:75). Every call walks the whole
  world again: `World["water"]` by dictionary lookup and an `EllipseRadius` per body, then every entry of `Fields`
  by `Contains`, then — on dry land above sea level, which is most of the island — `IslandWater.StreamAt`, which
  walks **every canyon with a full `Path()` polyline distance** and then every field a second time. Measured
  **7.5 us over the sea, 14.4 us at KSNA**, against **3.6-4.2 us** for the indexed `GroundHeightAt` beside it.
  **Needs:** the same bounded-cost treatment as the height field — a spatial index so a sample only visits the
  water bodies, fields and canyons whose footprints contain it, with an early-out for the common case of dry land
  nowhere near a stream. Target the same order as the height query. For scale: at 14 us a Pitts flying 10-20 m
  above the ground runs at **13 fps on an iPad mini**; the same flight 400 m up runs at 61. I have not touched any
  world file or the water geometry.

  at eight places — KSNA, mid-island, Drake, KMYL, 3U2's slope, Powell canyon, the sea and the PHDH hill —
  survives all eight with no NaN and no exception; and **sixty seconds of island flight is clean in the sim** for
  both the Pitts and the 172, worst single sim-second 288 ms of CPU on this machine. Ty's screenshot shows
  ordinary flight values at the moment it stopped (54 kt, alpha 61.4, 90 ft/s down, mid-spin, descending toward
  terrain), which is consistent with the frame stopping rather than the aeroplane. So it is above the sim.
  New `FreezeWatch` (always on, one float comparison a frame) prints a line for every frame over 300 ms and a
  heartbeat every 5 s, carrying where the aeroplane is, the camera's height above ground, the forest streamer's
  live/queued/worst, the bubble count and the managed heap — so a freeze that cannot be reproduced on demand
  leaves evidence instead of silence. `AERO_SELFTEST=perf` now takes `AERO_TYPE` and `AERO_START`, so the
  measurement can be pointed at the Pitts in the box instead of only the 172 off a runway.

- **[Claude -> codex] HANDOFF: the S3 thermal start and its lift centre are 1,200 m apart.** `starts[id=S3].centre` is (E 4.5, N -4.6) km while `lift_terrain[id=S3].centre` is (E 5.7, N -4.6) km. Codex's decision of 2026-10-31 is to keep the lift centre and move the start; both live in the world data, so the move is Codex's. Nothing is broken by it today — the start is 457 m above good ground — it simply does not begin in the lift it is named for, so a thermal start there is a glide. `TheOnlyThermalStartAwayFromItsLiftIsS3` holds the line meanwhile: it passes with this one mismatch, passes once the start moves, and fails if a second one appears.
- **THE APP OPENS AND DOES NOT PLAY — root cause confirmed and quantified, and it is NOT fully fixable in my lane (Claude, 2026-10-30).** It is neither a crash nor a hang nor a config failure. Build 2026.1030.2201 on Ty's iPad mini, launched through `devicectl --console` with `AERO_SELFTEST=perf`, which drives the menu's own FLY path: `StartMenu:Fly()` ran, the aeroplane spawned, the simulation ran and kept running. It ran at **5 fps, with 220–235 ms of CPU main-thread time per frame against 4–5 ms of GPU**. No exception, no NaN, no watchdog kill, GPU idle. The aeroplane flies; it flies far too slowly to fly.
  **Why, measured on this machine, one aeroplane and no AI traffic:**
  - `AirframeContact.Compute` cost **1,488 us per call** — 99 us for each of the 172's 15 contact points — against **37 us for the entire aerodynamic pass**. Contact, not aero, not graphics.
  - One island height query costs **~70 us**, because `IslandTerrain.Evaluate` walks the whole world description per sample: both coast polygons, regional overrides, crests, peaks, water, glaciers, canyons (a nested loop over every path segment, twice), lesson terrain and the outer islands. Its exact-coordinate memo cache cannot help a moving aeroplane, whose every query is a fresh coordinate.
  - The contact loop asks for one per point, and RK4 evaluates forces **four times per step at 200 Hz**: about **12,000 height queries per second of flight**, ~1.2 s of CPU per second, for one aircraft.
  - The 15 AI aircraft `CombatController.Start()` creates are **not** the cause: they only step within `ActiveRangeM` (3 km) of the zone. I nearly fixed that and checked first.
  **What I fixed (mine, measured):** `AirframeContact.Compute` now tests the footprint first — the ground under the CG and at four points on the airframe's own radius, five samples instead of fifteen per stage — and skips the per-point loop only when the lowest part of the aeroplane is more than 60 m above the highest of them. Airborne cost fell from **1,643 to ~655 ms** per second of flight (2.6x). `SkippingContactAtAltitudeNeverSkipsARealContact` holds the gated forces identical to the exact per-point test across 180 states — flat field, Drake's vertical north cliff, a canyon, the sea, upright, banked and inverted — because a shortcut that misses a contact is a worse bug than a slow frame.
  **Why that is not enough, and what needs you.** In cruise it is still **1.5x slower than real time on a Mac Studio for a single aeroplane**, and on the runway — where every one of your eight start airports begins — it is **1.9x**, because near the ground every point must be tested and each test costs 70 us. No arrangement of Claude-owned code makes contact physics affordable while one height query costs 70 us. **This is a blocking Codex dependency, handed off below.** Per the prompt I have not started the IFR or weather work, which is gated behind the startup repair.
- **[Claude -> codex] HANDOFF: island height-field query cost makes the simulation unplayable, at `IslandTerrain.Evaluate`/`HeightKm` (src/FlyingGame.Core/IslandTerrain.cs:58-130).** Measured on a Mac Studio: **70.4 us per fresh query** (20,000 random samples inside the ring), 16.9 us when ~90 % of them repeat and hit the memo cache. Every sample evaluates the entire world description, including `Shore()` against both coast polygons, every crest and glacier via polyline distance, and every canyon via a nested double loop over its path segments. The physics needs thousands of fresh queries a second near the ground and cannot batch or repeat them, so the exact-coordinate `[ThreadStatic]` memo at line 60 never helps a moving aeroplane. **Needs:** a bounded-cost height query — a baked height raster with bilinear sampling, or a spatial index so a sample only visits the features whose footprints contain it. Target on the order of 1 us. For scale: at 70 us the 2026-10-30 build ran at 5 fps on an iPad mini (220 ms CPU, 4 ms GPU); the same world at 1 us would leave contact physics at about 6 ms per second of flight. I have not touched any world file.
- **[Claude -> codex] HANDOFF is not needed for this one, it is mine, logging it so it is not lost:** `configs/atmosphere/regional-atmosphere.json` anchors two air masses to `airport:Bench` and `airport:Mesa`, which the island world does not have — `WorldTerrain.Airports` now comes from `IslandTerrain.World["airports"]` (PHDH, PANC, PATK, KSNA, KMYL, 3U2, KMEV, KPGA). The device log shows `[Atmosphere] regional config not loaded (unknown airport anchor 'airport:Bench') — uniform air`, so the whole regional weather model is silently off. Re-authoring it is Phase 2 weather work on this lane.
- **UNITY LIBRARY CACHES ARE CAPPED NOW, AND THE QUEST LANES DO NOT SHARE ONE (Claude, 2026-11-02,
  lane/claude-deploy-cache-cap).** `~/Library/Application Support/FlyingGame/unity-Library-<lane>` was 164 GB
  (12 caches; the four Android/Quest ones 24.7 GB each) with the disk 97% full. `deploy.sh` now touches its own
  lane's cache and runs the new `tools/deploy/prune-library-caches.sh` before every build: at most 8 caches
  (`FG_CACHE_KEEP`) and 80 GB (`FG_CACHE_MAX_GB`), oldest first. Never the current lane's cache, and never one that
  a running Unity, xcodebuild, bee_backend, gradle, java or Unity dotnet process uses (argv, cwd, the worktree in
  `-projectPath`, or an open file via lsof). That check runs again right before each removal. When over the size
  cap it first **trims** build output (PlayerDataCache, Bee, il2cpp_cache, BuildPlayerData), which every deploy
  `rm -rf`s anyway and which is 20 of an Android cache's 24.7 GB. Only after that does it delete whole caches.
  `--dry-run` prints the plan. A pruned lane's missing cache is recreated empty by deploy.sh, which means a full
  re-import, not a broken symlink.
  Dry run on 2026-11-02 at 10:59 PST, from claude-island-nav, with a Unity/xcodebuild chain running in claude-crash-test (kept: in use):
  delete inertia-b-deploy, inertia, codex-vr-quest, vr-stereo (47.8 GB); trim claude-vr-cockpit, vr-quest (20.4
  GB each), codex-crash-audio, claude-crash-water, codex-extra-wing-b (3.6 GB each). That would free 99.3 GB and
  leave 8 caches at 64.7 GB. With `FG_CACHE_TRIM=0` it would instead have to delete 8 caches, vr-quest among them.
  **Decision for you: a shared Android cache.** Not done, because it is unsafe here. Unity locks a project with
  `Temp/UnityLockfile` in the *project* folder, not in Library, so two worktrees whose Library is the same folder
  are not stopped from opening it at once. The four VR lanes run batch compiles in parallel (serialised only by a
  `pgrep` check, which can race). One lane would then load the other lane's ScriptAssemblies and import results.
  Run strictly one at a time, sharing would be correct (Unity re-hashes and re-imports what differs). It would also
  cost a full re-hash on every lane switch. The trim gets most of the space back without that risk: an idle
  Android cache drops to ~4 GB. If you still want sharing, it needs a real lock around every Unity launch, not
  only around deploys.

- **The StreamingAssets trap has a second mouth: `git add` on a tracked-but-ignored file exits 1 AND stages it anyway (Claude, 2026-10-30).** Reproducible on this lane: `git add unity/Assets/StreamingAssets/aircraft/j3-cub-like.json` prints "The following paths are ignored... use -f", returns exit code **1**, and leaves the file staged. So a script that trusts the exit code would believe nothing happened, and a mirror edit can ride into a commit without anyone typing `-f`. It nearly got me. There is a second edge too: `GlideTableTests.EveryAircraftPassesTheNewAirplaneProtocol` fails if you run the suite after editing a config and passes once you build, because `ConfigSync` regenerates the mirror during the build — so its result depends on build order rather than on the code. `lane/claude-config-mirror` is the cure for both; until it merges, an aircraft JSON change on any other lane leaves a modified-but-uncommittable mirror file behind.
